recent_posts.author: psawyerberlin
recent_posts.content_text:
Thanks @Ticoworld, great project idea, it really tackles a practical use case.
To your question: in CSR, each runner has its own small wallet that the operator funds once. It pays the runner’s transaction fees by itself, and any surplus can be swept automatically to the owner’s address.
CSR (CKB Service Runner) could also be a solution for the keeper refill you discussed with @Ayoub_Lesfer.
CSR lets independent full nodes run scheduled or on-demand jobs on CKB. Combined with QuotaCell, the split could look like this:
QuotaCell sets the limit: how much can be spent, by whom, and to which recipient.
CSR does the work: for example “when the keeper wallet drops below X, move Y from the Pocket to the keeper”, so nobody has to top it up by hand.
The cap stays enforced by your policy on chain, and the refill no longer depends on a single person or server.
The CSR testnet is fully operational, so you can test an integration there whenever it suits you. I’d be pleased to answer any questions.

president_tin:
unlike RGB++, where users can completely trust their own keys
This phrase didn’t age so well: on-chain contract exploits are exactly what Rosen tries to prevent by using standard contracts!
BTW Rosen Team reviewed our plan: all fine except the node part, they won’t accept operator-run CKB nodes and want 3+ public endpoints per chain for Watchers and Guards.
And that’s the issue we have been working on since then:
github.com/rosen-bridge/guard-service
Enough Guards on one provider and a fake deposit pays out
opened 02:40PM - 13 Oct 26 UTC
phroi
Hi Rosen team,
I've been reading the Guard, Watcher, scanner and TSS code for t…he CKB integration for about a year. This is the most important thing I found, more than all the issues and private security reports I filed so far. It's not a bug in a function. It's a property the whole bridge relies on. Nothing in the code enforces it.
## The gap
In the [July security update](https://t.me/rosenbridge_erg/63209) @zargarzadehm wrote for the team:
> The invalid events were successfully mitigated because guards operate on different independent data sources. Since Rosen requires consensus among guards, the attack was unable to satisfy the required quorum.
I agree, that's what saved it. My point: **this independence came from what each operator chose to configure, not from the code.** On `dev`:
- Each read goes to one configured network. For example, the [chain handler](https://github.com/rosen-bridge/guard-service/blob/dc3be8cad8981e0248580c5dc04931a09e478e2d/services/guard-service/src/handlers/chainHandler.ts#L119-L134) builds Ergo from the node or the explorer, never both.
- The shared [`verifyEvent`](https://github.com/rosen-bridge/guard-service/blob/dc3be8cad8981e0248580c5dc04931a09e478e2d/packages/abstract-chain/lib/abstractChain.ts#L164-L259) reads the block transaction ids, the lock transaction and the block info from that one network. The Guard signs whatever that network answers.
- [`default.yaml`](https://github.com/rosen-bridge/guard-service/blob/dc3be8cad8981e0248580c5dc04931a09e478e2d/services/guard-service/config/default.yaml) ships public URLs that every Guard keeps unless the operator changes them, for example Blockstream for Bitcoin, Koios for Cardano, the Ergo Platform explorer for Ergo.
- A Guard doesn't tell the other Guards which source it reads, so nobody can see when quorum shares one provider.
So if enough Guards for quorum use the same provider, one wrong answer reaches all of them at once. Watchers on that provider report it, as the 84 invalid events in July show. Quorum then agrees on the same fake deposit. In July the attacker needed a scanner flaw to reach this. With a provider under their control, they don't. July was already close to this: Koios, the shipped Cardano default, was [the source returning the failed transactions](https://t.me/rosenbridge_erg/63118). The Guards that rejected were the ones on another source. Had they kept the default too, quorum could have passed.
Every chain the Guard reads is affected. A fake deposit on any chain is paid from the custody of another.
You named this risk for Handshake. @mhssamadani, [in August](https://t.me/rosenbridge_erg/63500):
> There are other minor reasons that slow down handshake however, one is the handshake has not enough data sources and this will be a point of failure that should be mitigated before going forward.
I'm asking the code to apply the same rule to the chains already live.
## Two boundaries I accept
No obligatory full nodes. @RaaCT0R was clear [in rcs#2](https://github.com/rosen-bridge/rcs/issues/2#issuecomment-5969120694):
> I don't think we can expect every Guard to run a full node on every network for Rosen, as that does not scale well.
Makes sense to me. Everything below works with public endpoints only.
No map of what Guards run. @Armeanio wrote two messages on [2 October](https://t.me/rosenbridge_erg/64436):
> I can’t claim what anyone runs on their computer with any level of confidence.
>
> If I had access to know that would be much less secure 🫡
Agreed on the second line. Direction 1 below tells the other Guards only which public provider a Guard reads per chain, with a self-hosted node shown as "own node". Direction 1 does give every Guard the list of providers the others read, so a compromised Guard learns it too. The shipped defaults already tell everyone the likely answer, but it is still the cost of making the property visible. Direction 3 shares nothing. And Guard-to-Guard traffic is [encrypted on the wire](https://github.com/rosen-bridge/rosenet/blob/488671348bab0c2fa48f238d74077b3801eee662/packages/rosenet-node/lib/createRoseNetNode.ts#L103), so none of it is visible to someone listening on the network.
**Choice is not a cross-check:** the [three endpoints rule](https://github.com/rosen-bridge/rcs/issues/2#issuecomment-5969120694) lets operators pick different sources, then switch when one is down. Neither picking nor switching catches a source that is up and gives a wrong answer. Only a second answer, compared before signing, does.
## Three directions, from cheapest to strongest
I sketched the first step of each against `dev` to see its shape (type-checked and unit-tested, never run against a network). I can share the diffs if useful.
### 1. Make it visible
Each Guard exposes which provider it reads per chain (or "own node") and shares that with the other Guards as an informational message. Each Guard can then raise a health alarm when one provider is close to the signing threshold. At this stage nothing is blocked. The property from the July update becomes checkable instead of assumed.
Rollout: an old Guard logs the message as an unexpected type and continues, so this can be released without a coordinated update, as long as the message is rare enough to not trigger the warn-log health check.
Second step: the same rule can block, no signing when the approving set reads one provider. That needs the tag inside the signed approval, so a coordinated update like the September audit fix. A chain with one provider then has no approving set that passes. Whether it stops until it has two, as Handshake needs before going forward in your words, or keeps running as exposed as today, is your decision. If it keeps running, the risk stays as today: a fake deposit there can be paid from any other chain's custody.
### 2. Say no explicitly
Today a Guard whose source disagrees [never answers](https://github.com/rosen-bridge/guard-service/blob/dc3be8cad8981e0248580c5dc04931a09e478e2d/services/guard-service/src/agreement/txAgreement.ts#L274-L281) the transaction request, so dissent looks like "not scanned yet". The rejected event's reason [is still a TODO](https://github.com/rosen-bridge/guard-service/blob/dc3be8cad8981e0248580c5dc04931a09e478e2d/services/guard-service/src/event/eventProcessor.ts#L66). Storing the real reason is the first small step. Then a reject answer with that reason, on the same channel, shows a disagreement immediately, instead of noticing it later like the [Bitcoin fee ratio case](https://t.me/rosenbridge_erg/63583) in August.
Non-agreement already pauses an event for a turn. A longer hold is the state question below.
### 3. Second source before signing
`verifyEvent` compares its three reads, plus the confirmation status, against a second configured source from a different provider, at the extracted-data level. It signs only when they agree. For most chains a second URL of the same network type is enough. A few extra calls per event, so free API tiers are enough. This is the one that verifies the answer: one poisoned provider can't get a signature from any Guard that enforces, whatever the other Guards chose. Once enough Guards enforce, the payout is blocked. It catches a provider answering wrong, not a bug shared by every client.
Rollout: shadow mode first. With no sources configured nothing changes. In shadow mode the only new behaviour is a log line and a health parameter. Then enforce per chain. A chain with one provider is the same call as in direction 1.
What these three miss stays bounded by cold storage as today: a bug shared by every client, or a one-provider chain if you keep it running.
The same check in the Watcher would help operators too: a Watcher reading a wrong source reports a false event, then its permits stay locked until a rescan or a Guard operator returns them, as after the July invalid events.
## From the sketches
All three are changes inside this repository only.
- A built network object doesn't know its own name or URL today, so for direction 1 the identity has to be recorded where the networks are built.
- Directions 2 and 3 share one design decision. Today an event is confirmed, rejected, or has no status yet, and the waiting statuses exist only after verification passed. An event blocked by a cross-check has nowhere to go. Whether such an event waits, expires or gets rejected is the question to settle first.
## What I'm asking
Which of these directions (or another rule) fits Rosen's architecture for Guards?
If a design review helps once you have something, ping me. Thanks for the quick fixes on #23 and #27!!
Keep up the Great Work,
Phroi

topics.title: CKBolt: Connecting Bitcoin Lightning and Fiber Network on Nervos CKB

recent_posts.topic_title: CKBolt: Connecting Bitcoin Lightning and Fiber Network on Nervos CKB
recent_posts.author: longdevbf
recent_posts.content_text:
Hello Nervos community,
We are excited to introduce CKBolt, a browser-based application developed by TEX Labs, exploring interoperability between Bitcoin’s Lightning Network and Fiber Network on Nervos CKB.
Bitcoin’s Lightning Network is a Layer 2 payment network built on Bitcoin, while Fiber is a peer-to-peer, multi-asset payment and swap network built on Nervos CKB. Both leverage off-chain payment channels to enable fast and efficient transactions.
CKBolt brings these two ecosystems together through a unified interface, allowing users to explore cross-network asset swaps and direct payments between Fiber nodes.
Our goal is to make cross-network payment interactions more accessible while demonstrating how different payment channel networks can work together in practice.
Product Preview
image1919×1042 210 KB
The following video demonstrates the current implementation of CKBolt, covering Fiber node setup, payment channel management, cross-network swaps, and direct payments.
Key Features
CKBolt currently integrates several core capabilities into a single browser-based application.
1. Browser-based Fiber Node
Set up and manage a Fiber node directly through the browser without installing separate node software. Users can interact with their node and access essential Fiber functionality through the CKBolt interface.
2. Testnet Asset Management
Deposit and manage supported Fiber testnet assets, including CKB, cWBTC, and rUSD.
image424×619 29.4 KB
3. Payment Channel Management
Open and fund payment channels with the CKBolt hub, establishing the connectivity and liquidity required to interact with the Fiber payment network.
image421×630 51.7 KB
4. Bitcoin Lightning to Fiber Swaps
Swap BTC from Bitcoin Lightning Network into supported Fiber assets, including CKB and cWBTC.
image1339×817 48.9 KB
5. Fiber to Bitcoin Lightning Swaps
Swap supported assets from Fiber Network back to BTC on Bitcoin Lightning Network, enabling transfers in both directions.
image1399×890 54.3 KB
6. Direct Fiber Payments
Send and receive payments between Fiber nodes using payment invoices, with the CKBolt hub supporting payment routing.
image1424×901 53.5 KB
Technical Overview
CKBolt uses HTLC (Hash Time-Locked Contracts) to coordinate cross-network asset swaps.
HTLC combines hashlocks and timelocks to establish conditional payment commitments across different networks. The mechanism enables the swap process to follow predefined settlement conditions while providing a time-based refund path if the required conditions are not met before expiration.
By integrating this mechanism into the application, CKBolt demonstrates a practical approach to coordinating payment flows between Bitcoin Lightning and Fiber Network.
Demo and Resources
Live Demo:
https://ckbolt.texlabs.org
Video Walkthrough:
Team:
https://www.texlabs.org/
GitHub Organization:
https://github.com/Tech-Expansion
Note: CKBolt is currently a testnet demonstration. All assets and transactions shown are intended for testing and experimentation, not real-value payments.
Future Development
Our long-term vision for CKBolt goes beyond connecting Bitcoin Lightning and Fiber. We aim to evolve CKBolt into a broader interoperability layer that connects different payment channel and state channel ecosystems, while addressing some of the fundamental challenges surrounding cross-network payments.
One of the key challenges we want to explore is liquidity fragmentation. As payment channel networks grow, liquidity is distributed across different channels, nodes, assets, and networks. Even when sufficient liquidity exists across the ecosystem as a whole, it may not be available along the specific payment routes required to complete a transaction.
Our future development will focus on improving liquidity coordination, capital efficiency, and interoperability across these networks.
1. Perun Integration and Virtual Payment Channels
Explore integration with Perun, a blockchain-agnostic framework for payment channels and general-purpose state channels.
Perun introduces concepts such as virtual payment channels and generalized state channels, which could extend CKBolt beyond conventional payment channel interactions.
We aim to explore how Perun’s technology could enable more flexible payment relationships, reduce reliance on establishing direct channels between every pair of participants, and support more efficient utilization of existing channel infrastructure.
This integration could also open opportunities for more advanced off-chain applications, programmable payments, and cross-chain interactions.
2. Cross-Network Liquidity Coordination
A major challenge in multi-network payment infrastructure is the fragmentation of liquidity across different networks and channels.
We aim to explore mechanisms that improve liquidity discovery, allocation, and coordination between Bitcoin Lightning, Fiber, Perun, and other compatible payment channel ecosystems.
Potential directions include:
Discovering available liquidity across multiple networks and identifying suitable payment routes.
Coordinating liquidity between hubs and routing nodes to improve payment success rates.
Exploring shared liquidity infrastructure and liquidity provisioning mechanisms.
Reducing the need for excessive pre-funded liquidity across isolated channels and networks.
The objective is to make liquidity more accessible across connected ecosystems rather than leaving capital isolated within individual networks.
3. Intelligent Liquidity Management and Rebalancing
Beyond connecting networks, we want to improve how liquidity is managed within them.
Channel balances are dynamic: payments continuously change the distribution of inbound and outbound liquidity. This can lead to unbalanced channels, insufficient routing capacity, and underutilized capital.
We plan to explore tools and mechanisms for:
Monitoring channel liquidity and identifying potential bottlenecks.
Optimizing liquidity allocation based on payment demand and routing activity.
Automating or facilitating channel rebalancing across payment routes.
Improving capital efficiency while reducing the operational costs of liquidity management.
These capabilities could help node operators and liquidity providers make better use of their committed capital while improving the overall reliability of payment routing.
4. Expanded Multi-Protocol Interoperability
Expand CKBolt beyond Fiber and Bitcoin Lightning by exploring integrations with additional payment channel and state channel protocols.
Our objective is to establish a unified interoperability layer where different off-chain networks can discover compatible routes, coordinate payment conditions, and exchange value through secure mechanisms.
This direction would allow CKBolt to evolve from connecting two payment networks into an infrastructure capable of supporting interactions across multiple off-chain ecosystems.
5. Expanded Cross-Network Asset Swaps and Payment Applications
Explore support for additional assets, networks, and swap routes, enabling users to move value across a broader range of blockchain ecosystems.
We also want to investigate new applications enabled by interconnected off-chain infrastructure, including:
High-frequency micropayments.
Peer-to-peer payments across different networks.
Agent-to-agent payments and autonomous payment flows.
Programmable payments and application-specific state channel use cases.
Ultimately, we envision CKBolt evolving into a flexible interoperability and liquidity coordination layer for payment channel networks, helping improve liquidity utilization, capital efficiency, and access to off-chain payments across blockchain ecosystems.
Community Feedback and Collaboration
We believe that connecting payment channel networks is only one part of the challenge. Making liquidity accessible, improving routing efficiency, and enabling sustainable liquidity provisioning are equally important to building a scalable off-chain payment ecosystem.
We welcome feedback, technical discussions, and collaboration opportunities from the Nervos, Fiber, Bitcoin Lightning, and Perun communities.
In particular, we would appreciate insights on:
How can liquidity be coordinated more efficiently across different payment channel networks?
Could virtual payment channels and Perun help reduce liquidity fragmentation and improve capital efficiency?
What approaches could make channel rebalancing and liquidity provisioning more efficient?
What additional protocols, assets, and payment use cases should CKBolt explore?
We invite developers, node operators, liquidity providers, and ecosystem contributors to try the demo, share their feedback, and explore potential collaboration opportunities with us.
Developed by TEX Labs.
Thank you for your interest in CKBolt!

Send and receive payments between Fiber nodes using payment invoices, with the CKBolt hub supporting payment routing.

image1424×901 53.5 KB

Technical Overview

CKBolt uses HTLC (Hash Time-Locked Contracts) to coordinate cross-network asset swaps.

HTLC combines hashlocks and timelocks to establish conditional payment commitments across different networks. The mechanism enables the swap process to follow predefined settlement conditions while providing a time-based refund path if the required conditions are not met before expiration.

By integrating this mechanism into the application, CKBolt demonstrates a practical approach to coordinating payment flows between Bitcoin Lightning and Fiber Network.

Demo and Resources

Live Demo:

https://ckbolt.texlabs.org

Video Walkthrough:

Team:

https://www.texlabs.org/

GitHub Organization:

https://github.com/Tech-Expansion

Note: CKBolt is currently a testnet demonstration. All assets and transactions shown are intended for testing and experimentation, not real-value payments.

Future Development

Our long-term vision for CKBolt goes beyond connecting Bitcoin Lightning and Fiber. We aim to evolve CKBolt into a broader interoperability layer that connects different payment channel and state channel ecosystems, while addressing some of the fundamental challenges surrounding cross-network payments.

One of the key challenges we want to explore is liquidity fragmentation. As payment channel networks grow, liquidity is distributed across different channels, nodes, assets, and networks. Even when sufficient liquidity exists across the ecosystem as a whole, it may not be available along the specific payment routes required to complete a transaction.

Our future development will focus on improving liquidity coordination, capital efficiency, and interoperability across these networks.

1. Perun Integration and Virtual Payment Channels

Explore integration with Perun, a blockchain-agnostic framework for payment channels and general-purpose state channels.

Perun introduces concepts such as virtual payment channels and generalized state channels, which could extend CKBolt beyond conventional payment channel interactions.

We aim to explore how Perun’s technology could enable more flexible payment relationships, reduce reliance on establishing direct channels between every pair of participants, and support more efficient utilization of existing channel infrastructure.

This integration could also open opportunities for more advanced off-chain applications, programmable payments, and cross-chain interactions.

2. Cross-Network Liquidity Coordination

A major challenge in multi-network payment infrastructure is the fragmentation of liquidity across different networks and channels.

We aim to explore mechanisms that improve liquidity discovery, allocation, and coordination between Bitcoin Lightning, Fiber, Perun, and other compatible payment channel ecosystems.

Potential directions include:

  • Discovering available liquidity across multiple networks and identifying suitable payment routes.

  • Coordinating liquidity between hubs and routing nodes to improve payment success rates.

  • Exploring shared liquidity infrastructure and liquidity provisioning mechanisms.

  • Reducing the need for excessive pre-funded liquidity across isolated channels and networks.

The objective is to make liquidity more accessible across connected ecosystems rather than leaving capital isolated within individual networks.

3. Intelligent Liquidity Management and Rebalancing

Beyond connecting networks, we want to improve how liquidity is managed within them.

Channel balances are dynamic: payments continuously change the distribution of inbound and outbound liquidity. This can lead to unbalanced channels, insufficient routing capacity, and underutilized capital.

We plan to explore tools and mechanisms for:

  • Monitoring channel liquidity and identifying potential bottlenecks.

  • Optimizing liquidity allocation based on payment demand and routing activity.

  • Automating or facilitating channel rebalancing across payment routes.

  • Improving capital efficiency while reducing the operational costs of liquidity management.

These capabilities could help node operators and liquidity providers make better use of their committed capital while improving the overall reliability of payment routing.

4. Expanded Multi-Protocol Interoperability

Expand CKBolt beyond Fiber and Bitcoin Lightning by exploring integrations with additional payment channel and state channel protocols.

Our objective is to establish a unified interoperability layer where different off-chain networks can discover compatible routes, coordinate payment conditions, and exchange value through secure mechanisms.

This direction would allow CKBolt to evolve from connecting two payment networks into an infrastructure capable of supporting interactions across multiple off-chain ecosystems.

5. Expanded Cross-Network Asset Swaps and Payment Applications

Explore support for additional assets, networks, and swap routes, enabling users to move value across a broader range of blockchain ecosystems.

We also want to investigate new applications enabled by interconnected off-chain infrastructure, including:

  • High-frequency micropayments.

  • Peer-to-peer payments across different networks.

  • Agent-to-agent payments and autonomous payment flows.

  • Programmable payments and application-specific state channel use cases.

Ultimately, we envision CKBolt evolving into a flexible interoperability and liquidity coordination layer for payment channel networks, helping improve liquidity utilization, capital efficiency, and access to off-chain payments across blockchain ecosystems.

Community Feedback and Collaboration

We believe that connecting payment channel networks is only one part of the challenge. Making liquidity accessible, improving routing efficiency, and enabling sustainable liquidity provisioning are equally important to building a scalable off-chain payment ecosystem.

We welcome feedback, technical discussions, and collaboration opportunities from the Nervos, Fiber, Bitcoin Lightning, and Perun communities.

In particular, we would appreciate insights on:

  • How can liquidity be coordinated more efficiently across different payment channel networks?

  • Could virtual payment channels and Perun help reduce liquidity fragmentation and improve capital efficiency?

  • What approaches could make channel rebalancing and liquidity provisioning more efficient?

  • What additional protocols, assets, and payment use cases should CKBolt explore?

We invite developers, node operators, liquidity providers, and ecosystem contributors to try the demo, share their feedback, and explore potential collaboration opportunities with us.

recent_posts.content_text:
Pulling the JIT inbound path.
On release, if the buyer could not receive, the daemon opened a private one-way channel from the Twine Fiber node and funded it. That is gone. open_channel is no longer part of a trade. The RPC token no longer needs write("channels") or write("peers"). The daemon pays the buyer’s invoice. It does not open a channel, fund one, or rebalance one.
The next piece on that node would have been rebalancing, so the hub kept inbound and outbound in the right direction. Together with JIT, that turns the desk into a liquidity provider. A wallet then has to peer with this hub, stay online, and auto-accept a channel the desk opens. Fiber Studio and any other wallet that already has its own channels cannot just receive a normal payment. That is the wrong place for this.
A trade is an invoice again. The seller pays the hold from their own node. On release, Twine pays the buyer’s invoice over a path that already exists. If there is no route, the hold stays locked and the buyer sends another invoice with the same payment hash, after their own wallet has inbound. The desk does not learn the secret before that payment. It still does not store a Fiber key.
Channel opening, inbound, rebalancing, and splicing are moving to a separate non-custodial mobile wallet. The user keeps the keys. The wallet does the liquidity work, the way Phoenix does on Lightning, instead of the desk doing it. Other Fiber wallets can keep using Twine as a coordinator. This wallet is for people who want a non-custodial wallet on their phone and do not want to manage liquidity. We will provide that. Work has started. The research now is the right way to implement it.
What else changed in the daemon since that update
The take no longer carries a Fiber pubkey or a listen address. Any wallet that can make an invoice can take. The desk does not need to know which node you run.
The fixed payment-method list is gone. A post is a price, a currency, and a size. The seller types the account details into the encrypted chat. The daemon does not store them, and they are not on the public order.
The 15-minute payment window is gone. The seller still has 1 hour to pay the hold. The hold is still 36 hours. A payout still has to start at least 30 minutes before that ends, and a dispute still does not pause the clock. If the buyer has not marked the money sent by that safety line, Fiber returns the coins.
A post can have several open trades. Each take reserves its own slice. Another take is accepted while enough CKB is left.
If the payout does not route, the trade waits. The buyer sends a new invoice with the same payment hash. A failed payment does not settle the hold.
The public desk speaks to its own relay, wss://relay.backr.site. A relay that does not store the event is dropped. A relay that disconnects is woken. There is also twine-push: it wakes the phone, and the notification carries no trade content.
On a machine that also runs Fiber Studio, the desk node listens on RPC 8229 and peer 8230, so Studio can keep 8227 and 8228. The watchtower fact in the biscuit has to be node(""). A hex pubkey is rejected before a hold can settle.

recent_posts.content_text:
Sorry i have been busy elsewhere.Coming back to this after your latest update now.
Moving channel management out of Twine makes sense to me. It keeps the trading interface usable by other Fiber wallets and reduces the permissions the coordinator needs. Good to see the earlier changes around the buyer’s payment hash and payout recovery carried through as well.
I looked through the current code and found a few details worth addressing:
1. Both legs need to use the same hash algorithm.
The hold currently fixes the algorithm to SHA-256, while the payout invoice parser keeps the hash, currency and amount without retaining the algorithm. Fiber v0.9.1 defaults to ckb_hash, using Blake2b.
Matching the hash bytes alone is therefore insufficient: the secret revealed by the buyer’s payment may not unlock a hold using a different algorithm. I would carry the buyer invoice’s algorithm through to the hold, or reject unsupported invoices before the seller locks funds.
2. The outgoing payment needs an expiry tied to the remaining seller hold.
The 30-minute cutoff controls when a payout may start. It does not establish when that outgoing conditional payment must expire. The current send_payment call passes the invoice and fee limit, but no tlc_expiry_limit derived from the remaining hold.
I would explicitly enforce that the outgoing payment expires early enough to leave time to claim the incoming one, including if a channel closes. A late release where the buyer delays revealing the secret would be a useful test.
Related to this, hold_received_at is set when the daemon first observes Received. If the daemon was offline when the seller paid, adding the full hold duration to that observation could overestimate the time remaining. The deadline should follow the actual locked payment.
3. The expired-invoice recovery path needs testing with an ordinary wallet.
Retrying the original invoice after restoring receiving capacity is understandable. Replacing an expired invoice while preserving its hash needs more care: Fiber v0.9.1’s new_invoice rejects a hash already stored on that node. I would validate the invoice’s remaining lifetime before accepting the trade and document a recovery procedure that supported wallets can actually perform.
There is also a user-facing question that survives the wallet split: if the buyer has already sent fiat and the CKB payment never completes, returning the CKB to the seller leaves the buyer needing their fiat back. The dispute process should explicitly cover that outcome. Checking receiving capacity before asking the buyer to pay would help, although it cannot guarantee that a route remains available.

recent_posts.content_text:
Twine is a non-custodial desk for buying and selling CKB with local money. Orders, encrypted chat, and trade actions go over Nostr. The CKB moves on Fiber, between wallets the two people control. The local currency goes from one account to the other.
Twine does not hold the money, and it does not hold a key that can spend the locked CKB.
Why this exists
Buying or selling CKB for local money still means an exchange, or a KYC ramp.
The exchange that lists CKB is not permitted where you live.
To sell on a custodial desk, you deposit the coins into the exchange first. If it freezes or bans the account, those coins stay trapped until the exchange decides to give them back.
Or you will not hand over your passport and personal data just to trade.
A swap can move crypto for crypto. It cannot settle a bank transfer, mobile money, or cash.
How a trade works
A seller posts a price, how much is for sale, the limits, and a payment method. The method is only a label. Twine never talks to a bank.
A buyer picks an amount and pastes a Fiber invoice from the wallet that should receive the CKB. The secret stays on the buyer’s node.
Twine shows the seller a hold invoice for that same secret. The seller pays it from their own Fiber wallet. After that, the coins cannot be pulled back early.
The account details stay in the encrypted chat. The buyer pays the seller directly, uploads the receipt, and marks it sent. The coordinator cannot read that thread.
The seller checks their account and releases. Twine pays the buyer’s invoice. That payment reveals the secret and settles the hold.
If nobody settles, Fiber returns the coins to the seller when the 36-hour hold ends. A dispute does not pause that clock.
Looking for testers
This is an early testnet build. I need people to try a trade and tell me what broke, what lagged, and what did not make sense.
Join the group: Telegram: Join Group Chat
Downloads, for macOS, Windows, Linux, and Android: https://twine-web-alpha.vercel.app/
iPhone is not supported yet. Use testnet CKB only. Twine is the desk. Fiber Studio is the wallet.
The longer write-up, including what this build still does not do, is in Twine is up and the original PoC thread.

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | ckb-adversary: generic attacks on real CKB transactions, before you deploy
recent_posts.author: T_Silva
recent_posts.content_text:
In my own words
What it solves. Every CKB lock and type has to refuse the same handful of tricks: skim an output, ride a second cell along, swap a dep, reuse a proof. Most teams test that their script works, not that it refuses. ckb-adversary takes one real transaction your script accepts, tries those tricks on it, and tells you which ones got through and who would lose.
Who uses it. Anyone writing or reviewing a CKB script, before deploying: one command on a testnet transaction, or a GitHub Action on every change.
Why me. At LusoCryptoLabs we build on CKB every day: the Cellula names contracts on mainnet, a hosted Fiber LSP, fixes merged into Fiber. We built this first for our own scripts. In November it flagged the part of an RGB++ proof the lock was ignoring, the bug behind the August exploit, and we read it as harmless. I want a tool that makes that impossible to miss, for every team.
How I work. We use AI coding tools for much of the implementation. The design is mine: which attacks matter, what counts as a finding, and nothing is accepted until a test fails first, for the right reason.
1. Project Overview
Name: ckb-adversary
One line: a command line tool that replays a real CKB transaction your script accepts, applies generic attacks to it, and tells you which ones your script accepted and should not have.
Type: developer tool (Rust crate and CLI), open source.
2. Team Profile
Telmo da Silva (LusoCryptoLabs, Porto): author and maintainer.
Background: at LusoCryptoLabs, a small studio in Porto, we build on CKB: the Cellula names and wallet, a hosted Fiber LSP, and fixes merged into Fiber and other Nervos projects. We review CKB scripts, ours and others’, with reproduction tests.
Links: github.com/LusoCryptoLabs, lusocryptolabs.com
Contact: hello@lusocryptolabs.com, Discord: tecmeup
Recent public work from LusoCryptoLabs on CKB, in Rust: fiber#1708, fiber#1718 and fiber#1719, merged into Fiber; and a script deployment issue reported to Spore, spore-contract#77.
3. Project Background
On August 15, 2026, 16.59M CKB was taken from RGB++ cells with 1,464 forged Bitcoin proofs, and it went unnoticed for 80 days. Per the RGB++ Association, a verification result was checked for an error but not for validity. Changing one byte of the proof and watching the script still accept it would have shown it.
That test, and a few dozen like it, are the same for every lock and type on CKB. Writing them by hand for each script takes days, so most teams skip them.
Scenario: before deploying a new lock, a team runs ckb-adversary replay on one testnet transaction the lock accepts. For each attack the lock accepted, the report names the attack, the field it touched and who would lose. They fix those before mainnet.
4. Solution
Give it a transaction hash and the code hash of the script under review. It rebuilds the transaction exactly, applies about 30 families of attacks that do not depend on the script, runs each through the same checks a node runs, and reports only what the script accepted and should not have.
How it differs:
ckb-testtool runs your own tests and accepts transactions a node would refuse (no fee, under occupied capacity). This adds the node’s checks.
ckb-debugger runs one transaction. It does not invent the attacker’s.
Hand-written negative tests cover what the author thought of. These are the cases authors usually miss, the same for every script.
5. Technical Approach
Stack: Rust, on ckb-testtool and CKB’s own verifiers. Node checks adapted from iCKB’s VerifyRealistic (MIT). Output in English.
A verdict: rebuild the honest transaction and check its hash against the chain; apply each attack; drop mutants the node itself would refuse; run each script group on its own; an oracle flags a loss for someone other than the attacker, a cell riding free, or a broken stated rule; every verdict is compared with a stored file in CI.
Hardest part: a witness byte the script ignores is either harmless (a Bitcoin segwit signature) or the bug (a proof never checked). The report maps each ignored byte to its field and only allows fields provably outside every check.
6. To-Do List
Week 1: open the repository under MIT. A replay command that fetches a transaction by hash from a public RPC (mainnet or testnet), captures its cell deps as they were, and checks the rebuilt hash. README with a five-minute quick start.
Week 2: a report as a table and as JSON, with each witness byte the script ignores mapped to the field it belongs to. A GitHub Action and an example repository with a deliberately vulnerable script that fails CI, and its fixed version that passes. Milestone: v0.1 released.
Week 3: publish the list of scripts to test: the most used locks and types on mainnet by live cells (about 15). Collect one honest transaction for each and run.
Week 4: check every accepted attack by hand. A real finding goes to week 5. Noise becomes a fix in the tool, with a test, so it does not come back.
Week 5: report real findings privately to each owner. Nothing is published before a fix, or 30 days after the owner was told. Write the coverage table.
Week 6: final report, a five-minute demo video, docs. Milestone: v0.2 released.
7. Required Funding and Breakdown
Total: $1,000, paid in CKB. All technical work; no community or marketing spend.

A. Deliverables

Hi @Linet_Mugwanja, nice design! Anyone can trigger a collection, but the payout always goes to the creator. That leaves one gap: someone has to show up each period and pay the fee.
CKB Service Runner (CSR) can be that keeper:
Trigger: “every k blocks” or “at time”, proven via since, so no early runs
Service: reads the subscription cell, checks the period, returns the collection tx
Payment: the runner takes a tip + fee from a separate job cell, and the creator’s payout is untouched
Together with my note on Message in a Cell, that’s two good reasons to join CSR if you run a node: keepers for your own apps, and tips for your node.

recent_posts.topic_title: Message in a Cell: seal a letter, a photo or a video with CKB until a day that matters
recent_posts.author: Linet_Mugwanja
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi everyone! I’m Linnette from the CKBuilders program. After CadencePay ( CadencePay: recurring payments on CKB where the person paying stays in control ), here’s the other project I built: Message in a Cell.
The moment it felt real
A friend tried it and sealed a message for me. When the countdown ended I opened it, and the letter and the CKB were mine. It was a small thing, but it felt like getting a real letter, from a blockchain.
What it does
You write a letter, add a photo or record a video or voice note, put some CKB in with it, and seal it until a date. On that day, the person you chose opens it, and the message and the CKB are theirs.
It fits CKB naturally: storing data locks 1 CKB per byte, and opening the capsule gives all of it to the recipient. So the storage isn’t a fee, it’s part of the gift.
Three ways to use it
A gift: birthdays, graduations, weddings. It opens on the date, not a moment before.
If I’m gone: check in now and then. If you stop, it opens for the person you chose.
Future me: a letter and some savings to yourself.
How it works
A Rust lock script, capsule-lock, decides who can open a capsule and when. The date is enforced by CKB consensus through since, so not even I can open it early. It has 23 attack tests, and it fixes a time-lock bug I had in week 5. Letters and photos live in the cell, encrypted in your browser. You can send to a wallet, or as a link with a 4-word secret word.

Is my lock design sound, especially using since for both a fixed date and “no check-in for N days”?
Is there a good way to keep the message itself sealed until the date, not only the CKB? (I’m looking at drand timelock encryption.)

recent_posts.content_text:
Rivet Phase 1 Delivery Report
Implementation and project acceptance testing for Rivet’s first grant milestone are complete and ready for community review. Milestone 1 delivers GitHub-first onboarding, optional JoyID wallet ownership verification, sponsored CoTA identity activation, identity and backup-proof commitments in a user-owned CoTA tree, and Sovereign Passport minting on CKB Testnet.
The hosted acceptance run covered GitHub sign-in and wallet-free backup through identity activation, manifest claim and sync, passport minting, and public-profile display. Reconnect, unchanged sync, duplicate-mint prevention, independent proof verification, and profile-privacy checks have also been completed. The implementation and linked testnet evidence are submitted here for community and milestone review.
Repository: jedi-dtechmaker/Rivet
Hosted application: rivet-web-ten.vercel.app
Dashboard: rivet-web-ten.vercel.app/dashboard
Funded proposal and discussion: Rivet: Decentralized GitHub Backup, Timestamping and Restore on CKB
Milestone checklist: Phase One milestones
Latest implementation release in this report: commit ff5b040
Milestone 1 deliverables
The three Milestone 1 deliverables map to the implementation as follows:
Deliverable
Delivered behavior
Review evidence
CoTA onboarding
Rivet-sponsored activation creates a CoTA cell under the developer’s verified JoyID lock; the developer can claim and update identity and backup commitments.
Registration, issuer, claim, and update transactions linked below.
Optional JoyID connection
GitHub backups work without a wallet; connecting JoyID starts account-bound ownership verification before on-chain activation.
Hosted dashboard, wallet-proof implementation, and completed hosted onboarding checks.
Sovereign Passport
A verified manifest snapshot is minted as a wallet-owned Spore digital object, with saved mint plans, exact retries, and public-profile integration.
Passport mint, Spore ID, implementation, and completed ownership/privacy checks linked below.
GitHub onboarding and sponsored CoTA identity
Rivet connects repository backup evidence to a developer-controlled on-chain identity. GitHub remains the starting point: a developer signs in and can back up public repositories without first creating or connecting a wallet. The backup flow mirrors repository history, produces a Git bundle, pins it to IPFS, and anchors its commit-set commitment on CKB. Developers who want an on-chain identity can then connect JoyID from the dashboard.
Wallet linking requires a server-issued ownership challenge bound to the account, wallet, origin, and expiry. JoyID’s passkey signature is verified before the wallet is linked to the GitHub identity. An address submitted by itself is insufficient. The connected developer then activates a sponsored CoTA identity, with the resulting cell locked to their verified JoyID wallet.
The initial confirmed registration provided 150 test CKB of capacity through Rivet sponsorship. Users do not need to acquire that capacity themselves to activate their identity. Registration and transaction state are persisted so retries can recover the existing operation.
Sponsored registration: CKB Testnet transaction
Ownership and onboarding implementation: WalletIdentity
Server-side passkey and wallet verification: wallet-proof.ts
User-owned CoTA manifests and backup proofs
The CoTA manifest lifecycle now supports issuance, owner-approved claim, and subsequent backup updates. A dedicated Rivet issuer creates the metadata records, and the developer claims them into their JoyID-owned CoTA tree. Later updates add completed public backup proofs with explicit JoyID approval. The records commit the full 32-byte manifest root; the exported manifest provides the identity and backup records needed to reconstruct and check that commitment.
The manifest format is versioned as rivet-cota-manifest-v1. Its binding includes the CKB network, immutable GitHub account ID, owner and issuer lock hashes, collection ID, and two distinct token indexes. Developer records bind the GitHub identity to the wallet lock. Backup records contain the immutable repository ID, repository name, IPFS CID, commit-set Merkle root, anchor outpoint, and commit count. Record keys use immutable repository IDs so a repository name alone cannot substitute a different repository.
Two CoTA metadata records carry the complete root: the first characteristic stores 20 bytes, and the second stores the remaining 12 bytes with canonical padding. Verification reconstructs the full root and checks the manifest records against it. The Git bundle itself remains in IPFS.
Independent manifest verification checks the configured issuer binding, JoyID ownership approval, issuance and claim references, the reconstructed manifest commitment, and the referenced backup anchor through public CKB Testnet RPC. The verified backup snapshot contains one public backup proof and one verified backup anchor.
Issuer registration: CKB Testnet transaction
Metadata collection definition: CKB Testnet transaction
JoyID-approved claim: CKB Testnet transaction
Initial independently verified backup update: CKB Testnet transaction
Latest confirmed manifest update: CKB Testnet transaction
Verification procedure: CoTA manifest runbook
Standalone verifier: verify-cota-manifest.ts
Independent verification
The public testnet identifiers used by this release are:
Manifest collection ID: 0x8340e0bf4c432def07fef3bae8d46f43569bf4f8.
Trusted issuer lock hash: 0xf2834302ab71b9094c16c1507e9ce2289dade32b444491d557da1c439c8f8579.
Exported proof format: rivet-cota-manifest-proof-v1.
Record encoding and commitment construction: cota-manifest.ts.
Chain-based proof checks: cota-manifest-verify.ts.
Reviewers can download the manifest proof from the dashboard, independently compare the issuer lock hash against the public deployment evidence, and run the standalone verifier from the repository root:
pnpm --filter @rivet/web exec tsx scripts/verify-cota-manifest.ts \
--proof /absolute/path/rivet-cota-manifest-proof.json \
--issuer-lock-hash 0xf2834302ab71b9094c16c1507e9ce2289dade32b444491d557da1c439c8f8579
The verifier reads transaction references from the proof package and retrieves committed transaction data from the selected public RPC. It reconstructs the issuance, claim, and update lineage and checks each backup root against its referenced anchor output. It requires neither Rivet database credentials nor an issuer private key. A proof cannot select its own trusted issuer.
Backup sync and retry behavior
The dashboard shows one stored public backup, one synced proof, and no newer completed backup awaiting sync. Independent verification of the latest manifest and current passport ownership was included in the completed project acceptance checks.
Existing backups can be reconciled into the manifest without uploading another bundle or producing another backup anchor. Preparation also detects an unchanged confirmed snapshot before reserving another publication operation. Approved transaction bytes are saved for exact retries after an uncertain submission. Live acceptance confirmed that disconnecting, reloading, and reconnecting the same wallet preserves the synchronized state without another transaction or fee when the records are unchanged.
Sovereign Passport
The Sovereign Passport is implemented as a Spore V2 digital object owned through the developer’s verified JoyID wallet. Its immutable JSON content records the GitHub identity, initial owner lock hash, manifest root, and manifest transaction reference. The passport preserves the verified snapshot selected at mint time; a later backup update can advance the current manifest independently.
